description: Editorial description of the on-screen teaching sequence; not spoken narration. The soundtrack is music.

segments.text: A recurrent neural network processes a sequence one item at a time, carrying a hidden state forward.
Word order matters: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” contain the same words but express different events.
Map each token to an embedding vector before passing it to the recurrent computation.
At each step, combine the current input with the previous hidden state using learned weights and an activation.
The updated hidden state carries information into the next step. The recurrent parameters are shared across time.
Unrolling draws the same computation repeatedly, making the sequence of dependencies visible.
A prediction head converts a hidden state into scores for the next token; softmax turns those scores into probabilities.
Compare the next-token prediction with the true next token using cross-entropy loss.
A later prediction may need information that appeared several steps earlier.
The fading memory bars illustrate a difficulty; they are not measurements of the contribution of each word.
Backpropagation through time follows the dependencies backward to compute gradients for the shared weights.
Repeated multiplication can shrink gradients. Multiplying by one half repeatedly is an illustrative example, not a law that every recurrent gradient follows.
Updates based on weak long-range gradients may struggle to teach the network which earlier information to retain.
LSTMs and GRUs introduce gates that regulate what to retain, overwrite or expose.
The next section examines these gated architectures. They improve the ability to learn longer dependencies, while retaining sequential computation.
